title: Wire-arc DED of trimetallic HSLA-steel/CuSi/Al-5356 graded materials using a novel thermal management system
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces an active thermal management (ATM) system mitigating the thermal stresses associated with WA-DED of HSLA steel/CuSi/aluminum (Al) trimetallic structures. The study aims to regulate the formation of detrimental intermetallic phases at the CuSi/Al interface. Preliminary trials included quantitative porosity analysis and qualitative interfacial cracking inspection to obtain the appropriate processing parameters of Al-5356 on CuSi substrates. The developed ATM system enabled multi-layer deposition of trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al-5356 structures. Comprehensive microstructural analysis revealed a continuous 2 µm film of η-AlCu intermetallic phase along the CuSi/Al-5356 interface, and a 40 µm mixed zone of eutectic (α-Al + θ-Al 2 Cu) and intermetallic phases. Hardness measurement along the building direction passing through the interface between CuSi and Al layers revealed an abrupt increase in hardness up to (350 HV), which confirmed the formation of hard intermetallic phase along the CuSi/Al interface. Tensile testing of the trimetallic material along the building direction revealed a significant reduction in strength and ductility compared to the transverse tested single material samples due to the induced influence of the brittle intermetallic layer formed at the CuSi/Al interface. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Industry 5.0, formally introduced by the European Union in 2021, emphasizes the integration of human creativity and expertise with intelligent autonomous systems to achieve sustainable and cost effective manufacturing solutions that prioritize human welfare [ 1 ]. Recent technological advancements have opened new opportunities for this paradigm, particularly through enhanced human–artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration. Such collaboration enables in-situ monitoring and inspection of manufacturing processes, as well as the implementation of active control strategies, which can reduce material waste, minimize process deficiencies, and improve overall sustainability. A key aspect of this latest industrial revolution is the transition from mass production toward mass customization, which places increasing importance on flexible, decentralized manufacturing systems [ 2 ]. These systems are expected to enable the production of customized components with tailored properties, capable of meeting rapidly evolving and highly diverse human requirements.

Additive manufacturing (AM) is a transformative technology that enables the fabrication of highly complex geometries with reduced material waste and shortened lead times, aligning with the objectives of Industry 5.0 [ 2 ,  3 ]. Over the past decade, AM has evolved beyond its traditional roles in rapid prototyping and design visualization to offer robust manufacturing solutions for end-use customized products. This customization encompasses not only the production of components with user-specific geometrical requirements, but also the fabrication of parts with tailored material properties meeting the application functional requirements. According to ASTM52900-21, AM processes are classified into seven categories, where four of them are classified as metal additive manufacturing (MAM) methods [ 4 ,  5 ]. Among these, the two most commonly used categories for MAM are powder bed fusion (PBF) and directed energy deposition (DED) [ 3 ,  5 ,  6 ]. PBF processes offer relatively high dimensional accuracy and surface quality; however, they are generally limited to small-scale components and are associated with significantly higher operational and material costs compared to DED processes [ 6 ,  7 ]. Wire arc directed energy deposition (WA-DED), commonly known as wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM), represents a versatile and cost-effective DED variant capable of producing medium to large scale components [ 8 ,  9 – 10 ]. In this process, metallic wire feedstock is deposited layer by layer, using a welding-based power source, integrated with either a robotic manipulator or a computer numerical control (CNC) system [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ]. A key advantage of WA-DED over PBF lies in its ability to fabricate components with spatially varying compositions and microstructures, enabling the production of multi-material and functionally graded structures [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ]. By adjusting process parameters, locally tailored mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties can be achieved across the deposited volume [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 ,  18 – 19 ]. The research in this domain, commonly known as functionally graded materials (FGMs), is significantly accelerated by the growing industrial demand for advanced materials with location-specific properties in aerospace, automotive, biomedical, defense, and electronics industries [ 20 ,  21 – 22 ]. FGMs can be designed with either a gradual transition or an abrupt interface between constituent materials [ 12 ]. Abrupt interfaces can lead to significant mechanical stress concentrations and chemical incompatibility, potentially compromising the component’s structural integrity. Such structures with sharp property transitions are often classified as transitionally graded materials (TGMs), where the compositional change occurs over a few microns, resulting in distinct properties on either side of the interface [ 23 ]. However, the realization of these advanced materials is hindered by inherent process challenges. Residual stresses and distortion represent significant challenges in WA-DED arising from complex, localized thermal cycles involving rapid heating, melting, solidification, and heat source movement. These stresses are particularly pronounced during the deposition of dissimilar, multi-material alloys due to mismatched thermal properties, namely; coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE), and thermal conductivity. The underlying mechanism is governed by the temperature gradient theory: localized heating induces thermal expansion, which is constrained by cooler surrounding material, generating compressive stress. Subsequent cooling and contraction, similarly constrained, convert to tensile residual stress as the material yields at elevated temperatures. The thermal history evolves throughout deposition; initially, a cooler substrate creates steep temperature gradients and higher stresses, while heat accumulation in subsequent layers reduces this gradient and mitigates stress. Furthermore, previously deposited layers undergo cyclic thermal loading, which continually alters their stress state [ 24 ,  25 – 26 ]. Consequently, active thermal management strategies are critical to mitigate these inherent thermo-mechanical challenges in WA-DED, especially for multi-material deposition.

Steel/aluminum (Al) bimetallic structures are gaining increased attention in transportation industry aiming to reduce vehicles weight, increase efficiency, and reduce overall CO 2  emissions [ 27 ]. They are considered among the most employed configurations in shipbuilding aiming to enhance performance, cost, weight, and environmental impact [ 28 ]. One highly promising application is the fabrication of lightweight gears, such that low-stress zones are composed of lightweight aluminum alloys, while high-stress zones utilize high-performance steels. This strategic material combination enhances dynamic performance while significantly reducing overall mass without compromising functionality, driving substantial interest in the aerospace and automotive industries [ 29 ,  30 ]. WA-DED stands out as an efficient technology enabling the fabrication of these bimetallic components with flexible designs and tailored location-specific properties at low buy-to-fly ratio [ 31 ]. However, joining of these dissimilar materials often leads to the formation of detrimental intermetallic compounds (IMCs) at the steel/Al interface [ 32 ,  33 ]. Recent studies focused on mitigating or regulating the formation of these IMCs through process parameter optimization, alloying, or addition of interlayer between the dissimilar metals [ 34 ]. Kannan et al. [ 35 ] used cold metal transfer (CMT) WA-DED to fabricate steel/Al bimetallic structures. The low inherent heat input of the CMT process resulted in a thin layer of IMCs compared to blown-powder DED. The study demonstrated that the thickness of the IMCs formed can be controlled by modulating CMT process parameters to tailor the heat input during deposition. Extending on this, Abdul Karim et al. [ 36 ] demonstrated that specimens produced with lower heat input (< 117 J/mm) developed a thinner IMC layer (Al₂FeSi), which positively influenced tensile properties, however higher porosity was reported compared to high-heat-input samples. Raj Paul et al. [ 37 ] employed Al₂O₃ interfacial doping to enhance the 304L-SS/Al-4043 interface which resulted in grain refinement (~ 2 µm), and interfacial tensile strength up to 77.5 MPa with processing welding current. Raj Paul et al. [ 38 ] further quantified alumina’s role in SS/Al bimetallic structures, revealing tri-layered IMCs where increased alumina doping lowered elastic modulus but boosted hardness via oxygen embrittlement and grain strengthening, with peak tensile strengths near 59 MPa. Raj Paul et al. [ 39 ] also demonstrated the use of CuSi interlayer between 316L-SS and Al-4043 suppressing IMCs at the steel/Cu interface but forms brittle intermetallic phases (AlCu, Al₂Cu, Al₄Cu₉) at the CuSi/Al-4043 junction. The trimetallic SS/CuSi/Al-4043 structures showed an ultimate tensile strength of 62.71 MPa and a maximum deformation of 4.73%. Manohar et al. [ 40 ] deposited a CuNi interlayer between 304L-SS and Al-2319. The fabricated trimetallic SS/CuNi/Al-2319 structures showed a defect free bond between SS304L and CuNi, while the CuNi/Al-2319 interface exhibited a sharp increase in hardness indicating brittle intermetallic phases (AlCu, and AlCu 4 Ni), which pose challenges to ductility and toughness. Ahammed et al. [ 41 ] investigated the formation of IMCs at the interface of carbon steel/Al-4043 bimetallic structures fabricated via WA-DED. The study demonstrated that lower heat input (≤ 43 J/mm) produced a stronger interface with 54% higher strength (73 MPa) compared to high heat input conditions. Despite this strength improvement, the authors noted that continuous IMC layer resulted in poor elongation and extreme brittleness, indicating a need for further optimization by controlling the cooling rate, particularly for dynamic load applications.

To the authors’ knowledge, none has considered Al-5xxx series alloys in steel/aluminum bimetallic structures. Al-5356, widely used in WA-DED [ 42 ,  43 – 44 ], offers high strength-to-weight ratio and excellent corrosion resistance, suiting aerospace, automotive, railway transportation, and marine applications [ 45 ,  46 ]. Porosity and cracking represent major challenges during WA-DED of Al-5356. The predominant porosity in WA‑DED of aluminum alloys is hydrogen gas pores. During deposition, moisture, oxides, and oil residues on the wire or substrate surfaces decompose into water vapor, which reacts with the aluminum melt to produce hydrogen atoms, as represented by the reaction: 2Al + 3H 2 O = Al 2 O 3  + 6[H]. Although hydrogen has relatively high solubility in liquid aluminum (0.69 mL/100 g at 660 °C), its solubility decreases sharply in the solid state (0.036 mL/100 g). Consequently, hydrogen is rejected from the advancing solid phase and accumulates near the solid/liquid interface. The excess hydrogen is released in molecular form, primarily through heterogeneous nucleation on impurities such as oxides. These nuclei grow into bubbles by pressure and diffusion, expanding within the melt pool. Driven by fluid forces, including Marangoni convection, non‑isothermal flow, surface tension, buoyancy, and drag, hydrogen bubbles may either escape, reducing porosity, or become trapped, leading to hydrogen pore defects [ 29 ,  47 ]. Potential solutions to these challenges were investigated in several research articles, including deposition at relatively high interpass temperature, using low heat input power source, and addition of micro-alloying elements [ 45 ,  48 ,  49 ]. A few researchers studied the implementation of thermal management approaches, with focus on active cooling aiming at achieving higher cooling rate to obtain refined microstructures [ 50 ,  51 ,  52 ,  53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 ]. However, rapid solidification associated with high cooling rates tends to increase porosity typically originating at the grain boundaries of Al-5356 processed via WA-DED due to Hydrogen gas entrapment. In contrast, slower cooling at elevated interpass temperatures, where the extended solidification period allows gas bubbles to escape more effectively from the molten pool, results in reduced porosity [ 57 ,  58 ].

The present study introduces a novel active thermal management (ATM) system aiming to minimize thermal gradients upon the deposition of dissimilar alloys. Using the developed ATM system trimetallic high strength low alloy (HSLA) steel/CuSi/Al-5356 structures were fabricated. The significant thermal property mismatches between these materials including melting points, CTE, and thermal conductivities presented fundamental processing challenges, as summarized in Table  1 . The CuSi has relatively low melting point compared to HSLA steel so that it would act as a transition layer enabling the deposition of Al-5356 with relatively low heat input. The microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of the fabricated trimetallic structures would be investigated, with particular focus on the critical CuSi/Al interface. sections.heading: Materials and processing
paragraphs: Three feedstock wires, each with a diameter of 1.2 mm, were selected for the deposition of the trimetallic structures, namely; HSLA steel (ER110S-G), CuSi (ERCuSi-A), and Al-5356 (ER5356). Their chemical compositions are detailed in Table_2, according to the suppliers’ datasheets. WA-DED experiments were conducted at the Additive Manufacturing Centennial Lab (AMCL) at the American University in Cairo (AUC), equipped with a hybrid additive/subtractive manufacturing facility [ 62 ]. The deposition system utilized a Fronius TransPuls Synergic 4000 (TPS 4000) power source. A 6-axis ABB IRB 1600 industrial robot, synchronized with a 2-axis ABB IRBP A-type positioner, ensured precise and reproducible torch motion throughout the deposition process (Table  2 ). sections.heading: Bimetallic CuSi/Al trials
paragraphs: To obtain the appropriate processing parameters for the deposition of Al-5356 on CuSi, several substrates of CuSi were manufactured using additive/subtractive approach. CuSi walls each consisting of 22 layers were deposited on mild steel substrates with parameters adopted from a previous study by the authors of this work [ 63 ]. These walls were machined to specified dimensions (length: 120 mm, width: 20 mm, thickness: 5 mm), as illustrated in Fig.  1 . Active Thermal Management (ATM) was employed such that the CuSi substrate is fitted into a grooved steel block heating setup, as illustrated in Fig.  1 b, c, through which the substrate was pre-heated aiming to reduce thermal stresses between the dissimilar metals during WA-DED. Among a series of trials with the range: 150–350 °C, a pre-heat temperature of 250 °C was the most suitable for deposition of Al-5356 on CuSi. Lower pre-heat temperatures demanded an increased torch heat input for sound fusion between Al and CuSi, while higher temperatures would promote the formation of IMCs along the CuSi/Al interface [ 64 ,  65 ,  66 – 67 ]. Fig. 1 Fabrication of CuSi substrates  a  schematic of the deposition strategy  b  image of the as-deposited wall  c  schematic of the grooved steel block setup  d  image of the machined wall inside the heating setup

Building on this, a comprehensive parametric study examined Al-5356 deposition on the CuSi substrates, evaluating six distinct parameter sets (T1–T6). For each condition, three layers of Al-5356 were deposited using alternating strategy (Fig.  2 a) on a CuSi substrate fixed into a grooved steel block heating setup, as illustrated in Fig.  2 b, c. The experimental matrix varied welding current (75, 100, 125 A) and travel speed (18, 22.5 mm/s), while maintaining constant pre-heating (250 ± 5 °C), and relatively high interpass temperature (210 ± 10 °C) to decrease thermal gradient upon multi-layer deposition. All trials employed pulsed gas metal arc welding (P-GMAW) with high-purity argon shielding (99.999% at 15 l/min) to ensure consistent protective atmosphere quality. The three-layer deposition strategy was intentionally designed to capture the cumulative thermal effects, providing more representative data than single-bead depositions. Table  3  details the key processing parameters including: welding current (I w ), welding voltage (V w ), wire feed speed (WFS), travel speed (TS), with calculated metrics including: heat input (H in ), deposited material volume per unit length (DMV), and deposition rate (DR), which were calculated according to formulas given in Yildiz et al. [ 68 ]. A process efficiency of 0.8 was estimated for H in  calculation [ 69 ]. Fig. 2 Al-5356 deposition on CuSi substrates with the location of the porosity analysis sample highlighted  a  side view schematic with deposition strategy illustrated  b  top view schematic  c  top view image of Al-5356 deposited on CuSi inside the grooved block heating setup Table 3 Processing conditions of Al-5356 on CuSi substrates Trial I w  (A) V w  (V) WFS (m/min) TS (mm/s) H in  (J/mm) DMV (mm 3 /mm) DR (kg/hr) T1 75 17.5 4.6 22.5 47 3.85 0.82 T2 75 17.5 4.6 18 58 4.82 0.82 T3 100 18.1 5.8 22.5 64 4.86 1.04 T4 100 18.1 5.8 18 80 6.07 1.04 T5 125 19 7.2 22.5 84 6.03 1.29 T6 125 19 7.2 18 106 7.54 1.29

Mid-span samples were cut, using wire electric discharge machining (W-EDM), for quantitative porosity analysis and interfacial integrity inspection, as illustrated in Fig.  2 . The samples preparation protocol included sequential grinding with SiC papers, and final polishing with 1 µm diamond suspension. Panoramic images of the samples were captured using Zeiss AxioImager2 optical microscope. Quantitative porosity analysis was conducted on 3 samples of each condition, through computational analysis of panoramic micrographs using AxioVision software’s Multi-phase module, which provided the total porosity area ratio, pore size across defined classification ranges, and representative mapping of pore distribution within the deposited samples.

sections.heading: Trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al walls
paragraphs: Trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al-5356 walls were deposited for comprehensive investigation of the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties. The HSLA steel and CuSi deposition parameters were adopted from the authors’ prior work [ 63 ], which demonstrated defect-free bimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi FGM with robust interface. The Al-5356 deposition parameters were selected based on optimization trials of the CuSi/Al-5356, specifically condition T2 from Table  3 . The processing parameters for each material are listed in Table  4 . The process commenced with the fabrication of HSLA steel/CuSi bimetallic walls, with the deposition strategy visually documented in Fig.  3 . The as-deposited wall underwent precision machining to achieve final dimensions (height: 30, length: 120, thickness: 6 mm). The machined bimetallic wall (Fig.  3 a) would ensure compatibility with the 2-side-block heating setup, Fig.  3 e, f. Building on this, 15 layers of Al-5356 were deposited onto the bimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi walls with alternating strategy. Prior to deposition, the CuSi top surface underwent surface polishing and acetone cleaning, followed by pre-heating up to 250 °C. The 15 Al layers were deposited using 3-deposition cycles, such that 5 Al layers were deposited within each cycle. A heating cycle is applied after each deposition cycle to relief the thermal stresses, as illustrated in Fig. 5g. The interpass temperature followed a descending trend from 250 to 200 °C for each deposition cycle. Microstructural characterization began with sample extraction, using W-EDM, from locations identified in Fig.  4 . A rigorous preparation protocol was followed, involving sequential grinding with SiC abrasives (400–4000 grit), final polishing with 1 µm diamond suspension, and material-specific etching procedures. The etching regimen employed Nital 4% for HSLA steel, FeCl₃-HCl solution for CuSi, and Keller’s reagent for Al-5356. Porosity analysis was performed on the deposited Al-5356 layers, such that three samples from 3 different walls were analyzed using AxioVision software’s multi-phase module with the same setup followed for the bimetallic CuSi/Al samples. The Zeiss AxioImager2 optical microscopy system provided microstructural evaluation, while detailed microstructural and elemental analysis were conducted using a JEOL BT SEM equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). Five samples (X1 to X5, in Fig.  4 ) were extracted from successive locations along the build direction for phase identification and IMC detection at each region using Bruker D8 Discover X-ray diffraction (XRD) system. To evaluate the mechanical properties of the fabricated structures, tensile tests were performed for each material and for the trimetallic structure. Monolithic samples for each material were cut horizontally along the deposition direction (S1–S4, in Fig.  4 ), while vertical samples of the trimetallic graded structures were cut along the build direction with the gauge length including the three dissimilar alloys (S5, in Fig.  4 ). For the aluminum region tensile samples were cut at two different locations, namely; S1 near to the top most deposited aluminum layer, and S2 near to the CuSi/Al interface. Tensile samples were cut at location S3 such that the gauge length contains only CuSi, while the HSLA steel samples were cut at location S4, as illustrated in Fig.  4 . For each location, S1 to S5, three samples were cut using W-EDM from three different walls with the same processing conditions. The dimensions of all tensile samples were selected in accordance with ASTM/E8M subsize standard with a gauge length of 8.5 mm, and a total length of 32 mm. The uniaxial tensile tests were performed using Zwick Roell Z010 machine at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. Mechanical property variation along the build direction was investigated through Vickers microhardness testing using a Zwick/Roell DuraScan 20 G5 system, comprising 180 individual indentations for each sample (0.1 kgf load, 10 s dwell time) with 0.5 mm spacing. sections.heading: Active thermal management
paragraphs: The Active Thermal Management (ATM) system, shown in Fig.  5 , was developed to monitor and control thermal gradients during multi-layer deposition of Al-5356 on CuSi substrates and during the fabrication of trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al walls. The system employed four primary components: Custom made setup to ensure proper heat flow between the heaters and the workpiece (i.e. CuSi substrates, and Steel/CuSi walls in this case). Electric heating coils. Thermal monitoring system (including k-type thermocouples fixed at specified locations and thermal imaging to monitor the whole temperature distribution during deposition. Control device to trigger the heaters On/Off with specified frequency to control cooling rates during deposition. Fig. 5 ATM system  a  grooved steel block  b  two side blocks  c  thermal camera  d  thermal data acquisition devise  e  PC for temperature monitoring and control  f  temperature distribution during deposition with locations of the measurement spots highlighted  g  Temperature time curve recorded during trimetallic wall deposition

The custom-made setup is made of steel blocks containing the electrically insulated heating coils (2 × 300 W electric heaters) to actively heat-up the system during aluminum deposition. The temperature monitoring suite consists of localized temperature measurement at the critical CuSi/Al interface using K-type thermocouples positioned along the deposition path, while spatial temperature distribution was captured using a FLIR E86 infrared thermal camera synchronized with FLIR Thermal Studio software. Virtual sensors within the software, calibrated against the thermocouples, tracked time–temperature profiles at key locations. The heating coils were operated remotely via On/Off signals with varied frequencies to maintain the target thermal profile. It is noted that while the present study utilized this monitored manual control, an integration software will be developed in the future scope. This integration software is considered the fifth component of the ATM system, though which real-time thermal feedback will be integrated with location-specific heaters control, and WA-DED system for closed-loop deposition control. This would be realized via collaboration between human and AI models aligning with the objectives of Industry 5.0.

sections.heading: Bimetallic CuSi/Al trials
paragraphs: The porosity analysis results of the CuSi/Al-5356 bimetallic samples are presented in Fig.  6 , showing the relationship between heat input and porosity formation for each of the six tested conditions (T1–T6, in Table  3 ). Each trial consisted of three deposited aluminum layers, as illustrated in Fig.  2 a. The panoramic optical micrographs, Fig.  6 a1–a6, reveal the macrostructure of each condition, while the corresponding porosity color maps and overall porosity ratio (PR) are shown in Fig.  6 b1–b6. Fig. 6 Porosity analysis results for CuSi/Al-5356  a1 – a6  macrostructures  b1 – b6  porosity distribution maps with porosity ratio value  c  porosity size distribution chart

The results demonstrate that porosity decreases with reduced heat input up to an optimal value (T2 condition at 58 J/mm), reaching a minimum value of 0.85%, consistent with the reported values in literature on WA-DED of Al-5356 [ 43 ,  48 ,  70 ,  71 ]. Below this optimal heat input, the porosity ratio increases again. This indicates insufficient heat input, which resulted in a small melt pool and rapid solidification. This likely caused hydrogen entrapment, as gas bubbles had limited time to escape before solidification. Additionally, incomplete fusion and poor wetting at the CuSi interface may have contributed to microvoids and lack of fusion porosity [ 72 ]. In contrast, the highest heat input conditions exhibit transverse cracking and increased porosity, confirming that excessive heat input promotes defect formation [ 73 ]. At 106 J/mm (T6, Fig.  6 ), the large and unstable melt pool promotes keyhole pore formation. Although slower cooling rates theoretically provide more time for gas bubbles to escape, the accompanying higher WFS increases the deposited material volume, as evident in Table  3 , and creates longer escape paths, thereby hindering gas release. High heat input promotes the development of coarse IMC phases near the CuSi/Al interface. This structure is more likely susceptible to cracking under the high thermal stresses resulting from the mismatch in CTE between Al and Cu (Table  1 ). Accordingly, low heat input induced rapid solidification attributes to poor gas escape, while high heat input attribute to excessive hydrogen absorption and IMC formation, stress-induced voids, and cracking [ 74 ].

The porosity size distribution analysis in Fig.  6 c shows that the T2 condition contains primarily sub 10 μm pores that are uniformly distributed throughout the deposition, suggesting minimal impact on mechanical properties. This further confirms that T2 condition is the optimal for multi-layer deposition of Al-5356 on CuSi.

sections.heading: Macroscopic investigation
paragraphs: The resulting trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al-5356 wall, shown in Fig.  7 , demonstrated consistent layer deposition and interfacial integrity. This achievement demonstrates the feasibility of producing graded structures that combine the high strength of HSLA steel with the lightweight and corrosion resistance of Al-5356 through an engineered CuSi transition zone. Figure  7 a shows the deposited Al layers while still fitted the two-block heating setup, while the whole trimetallic wall after deposition is seen in Fig.  7 b. Figure  7 c represents a trimetallic characterization sample where the interfaces between HSLA steel/CuSi and CuSi/Al show appropriate integrity. Figure  7 d and e present the tensile samples, namely; trimetallic vertical sample “S5”, and single material samples “S1–S4”, respectively. Fig. 7 Macro-images of the fabricated trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al-5356 structures  a  trimetallic wall inside the heating setup during deposition  b  trimetallic wall after extraction from the heating setup  c  trimetallic sample cut from the deposited wall  d  trimetallic tensile sample “S5, Fig.  4 ”  e  monolithic tensile samples “S1–S4, Fig.  4 ”

Figure  8  presents the porosity analysis results for the trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al structures. A total porosity ratio (PR) of 0.75% ± 0.11% is determined, which aligns with the reported value of condition T2 (Table  3 ). The investigated samples showed a decrease in the porosity percentage and size along the build direction, as evident in the porosity distribution mapping presented in Fig.  8 a. These porosities would represent critical stress concentration factors near to the CuSi/Al-5356 interface. The effect of these pores would be evident during tensile testing of horizontal Al samples “S2” near to the CuSi/Al. Fig. 8 Porosity analysis of the Al-5356 region within the trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al structure  a  porosity distribution map  b  HSLA steel/CuSi/Al-5356 wall  b  porosity size distribution chart

sections.heading: XRD
paragraphs: The XRD analysis results, presented in Fig.  9 , reveals the graded phase evolution across the build direction (samples: X1 to X5, Fig.  4 ). The HSLA steel region shows a dominant ferrite (BCC) phase, while the CuSi region consists primarily of ε-copper (FCC). At the HSLA steel/CuSi interface, both ferrite and ε-copper phases coexist, demonstrating effective bonding without IMC formation. The Al-5356 region exhibits an α-Al (FCC) matrix with dispersed β-Al₃Mg₂ precipitates, while the CuSi/Al interface contains Al₂Cu and AlCu IMCs alongside the primary aluminum and copper phases. These IMCs, while potentially beneficial for interfacial strength, require careful thermal management due to their brittle nature. The absence of harmful Fe-Al IMCs at the HSLA/CuSi interface confirms the effectiveness of the CuSi interlayer as a diffusion barrier, consistent with previous findings [ 39 ,  63 ]. The relatively low heat input (~ 58 J/mm) and high cooling rate associated with the WA-DED process promotes the formation of Al 2 Cu (θ-phase) and AlCu (η-phase) at the CuSi/Al interface owing to the low activation energies (83.3 and 112.8 kJ/mol, respectively) of those IMCs compared to other potential phases [ 65 ,  75 ]. Fig. 9 XRD patterns of:  a  Al-5356 region  b  CuSi/Al-5356 interface  c  CuSi region  d  HSLA steel/CuSi interface  e  HSLA steel region

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: A panoramic image of the microstructure sample, labelled “M” in Fig.  4 , extracted from the trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al-5356 wall is depicted in Fig.  10 a. The microstructure analysis of the HSLA steel region adjacent to the CuSi interface reveals a characteristic ferritic structure, Fig.  10 f, which maintain consistent morphology throughout the build direction. Polygonal, quasi-polygonal, and acicular ferrite dominate the HSLA steel zone which is consistent with previous findings [ 63 ]. Fig. 10 Microstructure evolution of the trimetallic HSLA St/CuSi/Al-5356 walls  a  panoramic image of the whole trimetallic sample  b – e  Al-5356 phases along the build direction  f  detailed optical micrograph of HSLA steel  g – j  detailed SEM micrographs of Al-5356 with highlighted EDS spots S1 to S4

The fusion zone of HSLA steel/CuSi microstructure demonstrates complex diffusion behavior between the dissimilar alloys. Fe exhibits significant diffusion into the initial CuSi layers, while copper diffusion into the underlying HSLA steel remains minimal. The interfacial region contains distinctive iron-rich phases forming both dendritic and globular morphologies, with their concentration progressively diminishing across successive layers. By the fourth CuSi layer, these iron-rich phases almost completely disappear, giving way to the characteristic elongated columnar grain structure of the CuSi alloy. This microstructural evolution suggests that the initial deposition conditions create a transient compositional gradient that stabilizes after several layers, with the iron diffusion being largely confined to the immediate interfacial region. The gradual transition from mixed to CuSi microstructure over five deposition layers provides valuable insight into the length scale of compositional gradients achievable through this WA-DED processing approach. More details of the HSLA steel/CuSi interface have been extensively presented and discussed by a previous work of the authors [ 63 ].

The microstructural evolution at the CuSi/Al-5356 interface reveals a complex interplay of IMC formation and diffusion-driven phase distribution. Optical micrographs at different regions of the aluminum deposit along the build direction are shown in Fig.  10 b–e, with corresponding detailed SEM micrographs provided in Fig.  10 g–j. Elemental mapping demonstrates asymmetric diffusion behavior, wherein aluminum shows minimal penetration into the CuSi side (exemplified by only 2.17% Al at position S4 in Fig.  10 i), while copper exhibits substantial influence within the aluminum region, with an average content of 27.47% Cu measured at positions S5 to S8 in Fig.  11 . These EDS results, summarized in Table  5 , confirm the unidirectional nature of the diffusion process. This behavior is due to differences in diffusion kinetics, solubility, and interfacial thermodynamics between the two dissimilar metals. Copper exhibits high diffusivity in aluminum, especially at elevated temperatures, because of its smaller atomic size (r = 1.27 Ǻ) relative to Al (r = 1.43 Ǻ) and its strong chemical affinity for forming Al/Cu IMCs [ 76 ]. This rapid migration drives the nucleation of a continuous film (2 µm) of η-AlCu IMC directly at the interface where both Al and Cu coexist with nearly equal amount, S3 at Fig.  10 i. Adjacent to the interface, a mixed zone (40 ± 10 µm) was identified (Fig.  10 e,j), consisting of IMCs (Al₂Cu and AlCu), and eutectic phases (α-Al + θ-Al 2 Cu). In contrast, the solid CuSi lattice presents higher activation barriers for Al atom migration, and the solubility of Al in Cu rich phases is comparatively low. Moreover, the Cu solidifies much faster (MP ~ 1040 °C) than Al (MP ~ 640 °C) restricting Al mobility compared to the liquid Al. As a result, the diffusion flux is strongly asymmetric: Cu readily dissolves and diffuses into the Al melt, while Al diffusion into Cu is limited. Thus, the observed microstructure at the CuSi/Al interface incorporates two distinct features: a continuous 2 µm film of (η-AlCu), followed by a thicker (40 ± 10 µm) eutectic/IMC mixed zone, which reflects the dominance of Cu diffusion into Al [ 77 ]. The relatively low heat input (58 J/mm) adopted in the deposition of Al on CuSi resulted in a reduced thickness of the AlCu brittle IMC film compared to surveyed literature. This reduced thickness would likely enhance mechanical performance of the fabricated structures [ 39 ,  40 ,  77 ]. However, the highly brittle continuous η-AlCu film, even 2 µm thickness, is expected to induce stress concentrations that may initiate fracture under tensile loading, as will be evident in the following sections. On the other hand, the 40 µm eutectic/IMC mixed zone is susceptible to liquation cracking upon multi-layer deposition. Repeated thermal cycling has significant effect on microstructure evolution and integrity of the WA-DED fabricated structures. It accelerates the formation of IMCs (AlCu, Al 2 Cu), promoting the growth of coarse plate-like dendritic columnar IMCs. This results in thickening the AlCu IMC film and eutectic/IMC mixed zone [ 65 ]. Partial melting of the eutectic phases (α-Al + θ-Al 2 Cu) is another significant challenge associated with repeated thermal cycling. Upon re-solidification, these melted zones often transform from discontinuous eutectics into continuous-strip along the grain boundaries, evident in Fig.  10 c, d. This likely caused liquation cracks that occur preferentially along the eutectic grain boundaries just above the eutectic/IMC mixed zone, as evident in Fig.  10 h. These liquation cracks are of minor fraction as the heat input and interpass temperatures were carefully monitored to stay below the eutectic temperature (~ 548 °C), as presented in the time–temperature curve (Fig.  5 g) [ 78 ,  79 – 80 ].Within the aluminum region, a clear microstructural gradient is observed along the build direction. The lower layers consist of an α‑Al matrix with dendritic (α‑Al + θ‑Al₂Cu) eutectics, confirmed by EDS analysis at spots S1 and S2 (Fig.  10 h). The concentration of these eutectic phases progressively decreases with diminishing Al content along the build direction (Fig.  10 c, d), eventually disappearing completely by the fourth aluminum layer. In contrast, the upper aluminum layers (Fig.  10 b) comprise an α‑Al matrix containing finely dispersed Al 3 Mg 2  precipitates, as verified by EDS analysis (Fig.  10 g, Table  5 ) and further supported by XRD results (Fig.  9 a) (Fig.  11 ). Figure  12  presents SEM images illustrating two types of cracks observed in the fabricated tri-metallic structures: minor liquation cracks (Fig.  12 a) occurring along eutectic phases at grain boundaries, and solidification cracks (Fig.  12 b) forming within the AlCu and Al₂Cu intermetallic compounds (IMCs) due to mismatches in thermo-mechanical properties relative to the base Al and Cu metals. The latter crack type is likely to have a more significant impact on the mechanical performance, whereas the former is expected to have a comparatively minor effect. Fig. 12 SEM micrographs showing the formed cracks in the fabricated tri-metallic structures;  a  liquation cracks,  b  solidifications crack at the CuSi/Al interface

This comprehensive microstructural characterization provides essential insights into phase evolution and potential failure mechanisms at this critical dissimilar metal interface, demonstrating the significance of ATM during the deposition of multi-material structures.

sections.heading: Microhardness
paragraphs: Vicker’s microhardness results of the trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al walls are given in Fig.  13 . The variation in hardness values along the build direction, presented in Fig.  13 a, confirms their direct correlation with microstructural evolution. The results reveal distinct zones of mechanical behavior aligned with microstructural features, particularly at the critical CuSi/Al interface. The variation in hardness values follows the expected descending trend from HSLA steel to Al-5356, except for the abrupt hardness spike at the CuSi/Al interface, evident in Fig.  13 a. Fig. 13 Micro-hardness results of the trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al walls  a  variation of micro-hardness values along the build direction,  b  average hardness values for each region within the fabricated trimetallic structures

The HSLA steel region maintains high values (260 ± 15 HV), supporting its load-bearing function. The slight hardness reduction compared to conventional wrought HSLA steel (typically 250–300 HV) can be attributed to the characteristic thermal cycling conditions inherent to WA-DED processing [ 81 ,  82 ]. The CuSi region exhibits a graded decline in hardness, consistent with reduced iron diffusion and transitioning microstructure. In this region, the progressive disappearance of iron-rich dendritic/globular phases corresponds to a descending trend in hardness from 160 HV near the HSLA interface to 105 HV deeper into the CuSi bulk. This gradual transition of microhardness values from HSLA to CuSi without abrupt hardness spikes confirms the absence of brittle IMCs along the HSLA steel/CuSi interface, consistent with the XRD, microstructure, and EDS analysis results. At the CuSi/Al interface, abrupt increase in the microhardness value is evident from 135 HV at CuSi to 350 HV, as highlighted in Fig.  13 . The CuSi/Al interfacial zone features two critical characteristics: A sharp peak (350 HV) corresponding to the η-AlCu intermetallic layer, as identified by XRD (Fig.  9 b) and EDS (Fig.  10 i-S3, and Table  5 ). A mixed zone (95–185 HV) at the Al bottom layers comprising eutectic structures (α-Al + θ-Al₂Cu) and IMCs, as evident in Fig.  13 .

The significant increase in hardness at the CuSi/Al interface underscores the critical importance of precise thermal management during multi-layer WA-DED of Al on dissimilar alloys. Proper thermal control is essential to minimize heat input and thermal gradient, which could otherwise lead to liquation cracking along the brittle IMCs. The sharp transition in hardness, from 135 HV in the CuSi region to 350 HV at the interface, correlates directly with the formation of the η-AlCu IMC layer (Fig.  11 ). Under uncontrolled thermal conditions, this IMC layer could initiate cracks in adjacent eutectic zones (e.g. α-Al + θ-Al₂Cu) due to their lower melting points. The gradual hardness reduction in the Al-5356 region, from 120 HV near CuSi to 75 HV at the Al top layers, aligned with typical values reported in literature for WA-DED processed Al-5356 [ 83 ,  84 ]. This reflects restricted copper diffusion and a return to the bulk aluminum properties, confirming the effectiveness of the active thermal strategy in confining interfacial reactions to a narrow zone (~ 3 layers). This control not only limits IMC growth but also preserves interfacial integrity, highlighting the importance of tailored thermal protocols for producing defect-free, multi-material structures via WA-DED.

sections.heading: Uniaxial tensile testing
paragraphs: The uniaxial tensile test results for the samples (S1–S5, locations illustrated in Fig.  4 ) are summarized in Fig.  14 . The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of HSLA steel “S4” lie within the reported range for WA-DED of the same alloy, while the elongation percentage showed considerably higher values compared to literature [ 82 ]. This can be attributed to the softening effect of ATM system and intentionally low cooling rates applied during multi-deposition. The tested CuSi samples “S3” showed UTS higher than the values reported in literature, while maintaining comparable elongation [ 85 ]. This reflects the strengthening effect of the dispersed iron phases inside the CuSi narrow transition region. The Al top region samples “S1” showed strong correlation with literature for both UTS and maximum elongation results [ 57 ,  58 ], which confirms the proper selection of the processing parameters. However, the Al bottom region samples “S2” showed decreased UTS and ductility compared to S1 samples. This is attributed to the higher porosity density above the CuSi/Al interface as evident in Fig.  8 a, and would be confirmed via SEM fractography of the tested samples. These pores act as stress concentration factors that lead to premature fracture. Fig. 14 Comparison between the UTS and maximum elongation for the tested monolithic horizontal (S1 to S4), and vertical trimetallic (S5) samples

The vertical trimetallic sample “S5” showed significantly lower UTS and elongation than monolithic samples (S1 to S4). This is attributed to the continuous brittle IMC phases along the CuSi/Al interface [ 39 ,  40 ,  77 ]. The low UTS (45 MPa) and maximum elongation (4.5%) values of S5 samples are aligned with literature tackling the same challenges of the detrimental IMC phases along the Cu/Al interface [ 37 ,  41 ]. This requires further investigation through post heat treatments or interlayer hot rolling to mitigate the detrimental effect of these IMC and minimize porosity defects that contribute to stress concentration and crack initiation of the trimetallic samples.

SEM micrographs of the fractured surfaces are presented in Fig.  15  for different tested samples (S1–S5). The results align with the data reported in Fig.  14 . The ductile fracture mode of the HSLA steel samples is evident through the fine dense dimples shown in Fig.  15 d. The ductile fracture of the CuSi samples are evident in Fig.  15 c although some micro pores persist, dense dimples dominate the fractured surfaces. Figure  15  a shows the fracture mode of sample “S1: Al-top”, dominated by dense dimples, however micro pores and quasi-cleavage surfaces do persist. The less dimple density in sample “S2: Al-bottom” compared to “S1” indicate premature failure. This premature fracture originated a deep crack around a gas pore (100–250 µm), evident in Fig.  15 b, and aligning with the tensile testing results presented in Fig.  15  together with porosity analysis results presented earlier in Fig.  8 . The vertical trimetallic sample “S5” shows minor dimples, evident in Fig.  15 e and f, confirming brittle fracture mode with minimal plastic deformation (4.5% max elongation). EDS of the fractured surfaces shows higher Al concentration compared to Cu. This indicates that fracture occurred within the mixed zone (eutectic/IMC phases) just above the continuous brittle η-AlCu film. This aligns with the likely transgranular failure mode evident in Fig.  15 f. The fracture likely occurs within the dendritic Al 2 Cu phases as seen in Fig.  15 e (fractured dendrites). The growth of these dendritic, columnar plate-like Al 2 Cu phases (just above the η-AlCu brittle film) likely results from repeated thermal cycles associated with multiple layer deposition [ 65 ]. This transformation from FCC (Al and Cu) to BCT (Al 2 Cu) with the growth of Al 2 Cu (BCT) under relatively fast cooling rates (a characteristic of WA-DED process) may have initiated residual stresses due to the volume increase associated with the lattice transformation from FCC to BCT. Although the fracture occurs within the Al 2 Cu at the mixed eutectic/IMC zone, the effect of the brittle η-AlCu should not be overlooked. Solidification cracks propagating through the brittle AlCu and Al₂Cu IMCs at the interface arising due to the mismatch in thermo‑mechanical properties between the IMCs, combined with thermal stresses at the CuSi/Al interface act as stress concentration factors that likely have major effect on the mechanical performance of the fabricated structures. While, liquation cracks are of low volume fraction and they did not contribute to the fracture of the tested samples. Fig. 15 SEM micrographs of the fractured surfaces at low and high magnifications  a  S1: Al-top,  b  S2: Al-bottom,  c  S3: CuSi,  d  S4: HSLA steel,  e  S5: trimetallic Al side,  f  S5: trimetallic Cu side

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The novel active thermal management (ATM) system successfully enables the multi-layer deposition of dissimilar metals with significantly mismatched thermal properties such as melting points, coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE), and thermal conductivity by effectively minimizing thermal gradients during the process. Sound deposition of Al-5356 on CuSi is achieved using a heat input of 58 J/mm, pre-heat temperature of 250 °C and interpass temperature following a decreasing trend (250–200 °C), resulting in a low total porosity ratio of approximately 0.75% to 0.85%. Porosity formed in the mixed zone just above the CuSi/Al interface negatively affects mechanical properties, leading to lower tensile strength and ductility in the bottom aluminum layers compared to the top layers. A continuous 2 µm layer of η-AlCu IMC forms, bounded by a ~ 40 ± 10 µm mixed zone with (α-Al + θ-Al₂Cu) eutectics and Al₂Cu/AlCu intermetallic phases, as evident by XRD, SEM/EDS elemental analysis, and micro-hardness measurements. The HSLA steel/CuSi interface exhibits a gradual hardness transition (260 → 135 HV), whereas the CuSi/Al interface shows abrupt hardness fluctuations (135 → 350 → 185 HV) followed by a gradual decrease to 75 HV after three Al layers, indicating the presence of a continuous IMC layer at the dissimilar alloy boundary. The trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al samples exhibit poor mechanical performance (UTS: 45 MPa; elongation: 4.5%) due to brittle intermetallic compounds at the CuSi/Al interface. In contrast, horizontal HSLA steel samples demonstrate moderate strength and good ductility (UTS: 700 MPa; elongation: 35%), influenced by softening from repeated thermal cycles. Meanwhile, horizontal CuSi samples show relatively high strength (UTS: 400 MPa), attributed to strengthening from dispersed iron phases in the transition layer. In the future scope, post heat treatments and interlayer rolling would be examined aiming to enhance the fabricated trimetallic HSLA steel/CuSi/Al structures especially within the critical CuSi/Al interface. The ATM system will be further developed to apply in-situ control over the process thermal distribution according to the data acquired via thermal imaging and integrated with the WA-DED system. This would be realized via collaboration between human and AI models aligning with the objectives of Industry 5.0.
